extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; communications scholars; public relations historians
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the historical evolution, definitions, and core principles of public relations (including origins of the press release and major tactical/ethical lessons) intended to inform practice and teaching of PR. Covers one-way vs two-way models, management counseling, tactics, and the role of performance and truthfulness in PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and merit as foundation of effective public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective public relations depends on actual performance and merit; substantive organizational performance determines the publicity a client gets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Westinghouse's AC system won public acceptance despite Edison’s scare campaign, demonstrating that 'performance and merit are the foundation stones of effective public relations.' Anti-pattern: relying solely on spin when underlying performance or product is poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way (persuasion/propaganda) vs two-way (reciprocal) communication models
rubrics_metrics.description: One-way public relations emphasizes persuasive communication and propaganda (publicity aimed at influencing others). Two-way public relations emphasizes exchange, reciprocity, mutual understanding, and communication between organization and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way: press agentry and propaganda; Two-way: includes notions such as 'reciprocal, mutual, and between' and appears in dictionary definitions (e.g., 'The art or science of developing reciprocal understanding and goodwill'). Contemporary practice increasingly includes two-way communication, management participation, and corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as counseling/management-level function (adjustment concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR's role includes counseling organization leaders and influencing policy—helping organizations adjust their behavior to their social environment and reconcile aspects of behavior that have social significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted by professional bodies (IPRA) as including 'counseling organization leaders' and 'planned programs of action.' Implication: PR should be involved in corrective action, not only message delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ivy Lee's Declaration of Principles (openness and supplying news)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR work should be done in the open, supply news, not function as advertising, be accurate, supply further details promptly, and assist editors in verifying statements of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lee's mailed statement to city editors: 'This is not a secret press bureau ... Our matter is accurate. Further details on any subject treated will be supplied promptly, and any editor will be assisted most cheerfully in verifying directly any statement of fact.' Practice implication: use handouts/press releases to provide prompt, accurate information; avoid deceptive secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and avoiding untruths
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not issue untruths in public statements because they will be challenged as soon as they see the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lee's counsel: untruths are self-defeating. Principle supports ethics and long-term credibility; anti-pattern: issuing falsehoods to avoid short-term criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press releases/handouts as a journalistic facilitation tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Handouts (now called press releases or news releases) supply reporters with newsworthy material after meetings or events and simplify reporters' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lee used handouts to provide reports after meetings when reporters couldn't attend; practice implication: well-crafted handouts can generate favorable press coverage by making accurate information available to media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized public relations bureau functions (collect/analyze/distribute and monitor opinion/legislation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A centralized PR bureau should concentrate all information concerning relations to the public, collate scattered material, make it available, monitor trends in public opinion and legislation, and inform executives to enable timely responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AT&T proposal (1912) example: central organization saves duplication, provides broader/efficient treatment of problems, enables forestalling legislation by remedying conditions causing trouble, and keeps everyone in touch with national trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of publicity drives, decentralized mobilization, and mass-based tactics (Creel Committee model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale campaigns can mobilize public opinion through decentralized networks and mass messaging (e.g., Four Minutemen, drives for bonds or membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creel Committee used volunteers, decentralized groups, and coordinated drives to dramatically increase Red Cross membership and bondholders. Guidance: organize grassroots and networked outreach for broad mobilization; demonstrates PR's capacity for social influence (and ethical concerns about propaganda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of research and measurement of program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practitioners should employ research methods and measure program effectiveness to evaluate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendleton Dudley recognized the need to measure program effectiveness; practice implication: incorporate research, metrics, and evaluation into PR campaigns rather than relying only on anecdote or impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grassroots advocacy and third-party endorsement as persuasive tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics such as grassroots advocacy groups and securing third-party endorsements can be effective in shaping public acceptance and promoting products or causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carl Byoir popularized grassroots advocacy and third-party endorsement, and used methods like full-page editorial advertisements and promotion campaigns (e.g., Jeep, tubeless tire). Consider reputation and authenticity of third parties to avoid backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as defensive/offensive tool for business interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses historically used PR to defend themselves against investigative journalism and to counter regulatory pressures by telling their side of the story and counterattacking to influence public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early 1900s strategy: attempt to prevent regulation by shaping public opinion; anti-pattern: secretive or manipulative press-agentry that ignores public concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and reputational limits of client representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing controversial or harmful clients can damage a practitioner's reputation and raise ethical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ivy Lee's advisory role to I.G. Farben and perceived association with Nazi interests led to sensational headlines and criticism. Guidance: weigh ethical implications and long-term reputational risk when accepting accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When mutual understanding is insufficient, corrective action and mutual adjustment are required
rubrics_metrics.description: As publics become empowered and demand change, PR must go beyond mutual understanding to recommend and implement corrective organizational changes (mutual adjustment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical shift post-1960s: social protest movements required organizations to take corrective action. Practice implication: PR counsel should include recommending internal changes, policies, or remedies to address public concerns.
